newsitem.title: PERU: Peru having trouble selling key mineral assets.
newsitem.headline: Peru having trouble selling key mineral assets.

text.p: Battered by a hostage siege and tax worries, state-run Minero Peru's 1997 privatization program has limped from one delay to another, but officials remain unbowed and claim they will finish the year with a bang.

Minero Peru is "absolutely certain" it will sell by year end the large Michiquillay and Las Bambas copper projects as well as the Bayovar phosphate deposit, company president Jorge Kawamura said in an interview.
"The plan to privatize Minero Peru has not changed. We are doing promotions so that we can have a sort of relaunching of the sales," Kawamura said.
The success of Centromin in privatizing its operative assets has eclipsed the state's second miner, but the three upcoming sales will turn the spotlight back on Minero Peru, he said.
The upbeat message, however, is nothing new to potential buyers, who have been waiting for almost a year for the government to fix a date for the three auctions.

Officials claimed throughout the fourth quarter of 1996 that Minero Peru would sell Bayovar in February and then ride a tide of international interest to sell five more assets in 1997, attracting hundreds of millions of dollars in investment.
But Minero Peru has not sold a single deposit this year.
"Two months more or two months less does not really matter to the investor. What matters is that the conditions are right for the sale," Kawamura said.
Heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels blew a hole in Minero Peru's first quarter plans by storming the Japanese amabassador's home and holding 72 hostages for four months.
"For all the official talk that the hostage crisis did not affect questions of investment, it did in fact have an influence," Kawamura said.

But while Minero Peru was fretting over investor concern for country risk, Centromin attracted the world's top silver producer to spend $185 million for control of the state's largest mining asset -- the La Oroya metallurgic complex.

Two months after Peruvian troops crushed the hostage siege, Minero Peru still finds itself unable to lure investors to its auctions because the government has failed to push through planned tax legislation demanded by potential buyers.

Last week, the absence of tax breaks to improve cash-flow at early investment stages forced Minero Peru to put back the July sale of Michiquillay, which needs up to an estimated $500 million in front-end spending.
But analysts said Minero Peru's scheduled sale was also badly timed as Centromin had already slated the auction of its attractive Mahr Tunel production units for the same month.

"Mahr Tunel has attracted more interest than expected. It was logical to postpone Michiquillay because it is better to sell one asset at a time to concentrate investors' interest," said Guillermo Arbe, head of Lima research at Morgan Grenfell.
Mexico's Industrias Penoles, Switzerland's Glencore, Australia's Savage, Mexico's Grupo Mexico, the United State's Sunshine and Sweden's Boliden are all set to bid for the asset.

Minero Peru, which started its sell-off program in 1992 and offloaded the lion's share of its properties, planned to relaunch its sales this year's after it saw the steady success of Centromin's sweeping 1996 program.
But selling deposits that need long-term investment has proved much more difficult than privatizing already-operative assets.
"What Centromin sells are businesses that are already up and running. It is much more difficult to attract interest for projects," Kawamura said.

There are no dates set for any of its planned sales, but there are seven U.S., Canadian and Japanese firms interested in the Michiquillay sale and a further 25 companies lining up for Bayovar, according to the government.
Six companies are also interested in buying Las Bambas despite a legal dispute with the United States' Phelps Dodge over ownership, Minero Peru said.
((-- Lima newsroom, 511 221-2134))
